device.name: Bluetooth LED Name Badge
device.notes: Monochrome LED dot-matrix name badge. Sold under many brands on AliExpress. Matrix height 11, 12, or 16 rows; width is variable per text/image content. All three heights are fully supported app-side (its data builder handles 16 rows, and it bundles 16-row font assets ASC16/HZK16/JPK16/KRK16/TWK16). Protocol is write-only in practice (no useful reads). Data is written in 16-byte chunks: a 64-byte header (4 chunks) followed by stripe-major bitmap data — the message is split into 8-column-wide stripes of `height` bytes each, and each byte is one row of 8 pixels, MSB = leftmost pixel. Writes are ACKNOWLEDGED (writeCharacteristic, NOT write_without_response), with a 3-second per-write ack timeout, 300 ms delay before the first data chunk and 25 ms between subsequent chunks. Up to 8 message slots with per-slot flash and marquee. NO CRC/checksum anywhere in the send path, and NO length prefix at the BLE write level (raw 16-byte chunks). Device stores messages in flash and persists across power cycles. No pairing required. The badge only advertises after the user enters BLE transfer mode (press the lower button twice; a Bluetooth icon shows on the display). Advertised name is filtered by contains("LS") (app-confirmed in its scanner and main presenter). The vendor app ecosystem is active; this spec is verified against a full static analysis of that app. NOTE: AliExpress sellers ship mixed generations under the same listings — a newer badge generation uses a different, AES-encrypted protocol (github.com/timhodson/ble-led-badge), not this "wang"/LSLED one. An open replacement firmware for CH582M-based badges exists (fossasia/badgemagic-firmware). CONFIDENCE: HIGH (full static analysis of the vendor app; cross-checked against Elektor Jan/Feb 2023 sniff, Nilhcem, FOSSASIA and Doridian). Evidence, by area of the app: its device constants (name "LS", service 0000fee0, char 0000fee1); its data builder (the 64-byte header byte-for-byte, and per-slot length stored big-endian via byte swap); its send mode (64-byte header as 4 chunks, bitmap zero-padded into 16-byte chunks); its main presenter (300 ms before the first data chunk, 25 ms between chunks, 3 s per-write ack timeout); and its BLE service (acknowledged writes — the write type is never set to write-without-response). No CRC/checksum code anywhere in the app; service 0xFEE7 and characteristics 0xFEC7-FEC9 are never referenced by the app.

exclusivity.recovery: Close the vendor app, and any other client holding the device, before connecting. Nothing needs clearing afterwards — no bond is stored on either side.

credentials.notes: Anything within radio range can connect and issue commands. Physical proximity is the only access control.

factory_reset.effect: No credential state to clear. Power-cycling drops the current connection, which is the actual remedy for the common failure mode: the device already being connected to another central.

steps.action: Remove power (or battery) for a few seconds and reapply.
steps.expect: Device advertises again and accepts a new connection.

methods.description: No provisioning step: the badge advertises only after the user puts it in BLE transfer mode (press the lower button twice until the Bluetooth icon appears on the display) and then accepts a connection from any central. There is no account, no network credential exchange and no pairing PIN, so a replacement client only has to scan, connect and write.

steps.action: Power the badge, then press the lower button twice to enter BLE transfer mode (Bluetooth icon shows).
steps.expect: Badge starts advertising as LSLED (name prefix LS).

steps.action: Scan for its advertisement and connect.
Connect and run the documented initialization sequence, if the spec defines one.

setup.notes: No provisioning. These badges are widely reported as finicky to connect: they accept one central at a time and often need a power cycle between clients. This is user-reported, device-side behavior; the vendor app contains no connection-management code that bears on it, so there is no app-side evidence either way.

rejoin.notes: Nothing binds this device to a network or an owner, so switching controllers is just connecting from the new one. If the old client is an Android or iOS phone, remove the device from the OS Bluetooth list as well — a cached bond can keep the phone reconnecting automatically and holding the single available link.

entities.name: Badge Display
entities.notes: No role bindings, deliberately. The badge has exactly one write — `write_badge_data`, the 16-byte chunk stream — and it is not a control a role can name: the whole display, brightness included, arrives as the 64-byte header of a bitmap upload, which is what `protocol_handler: ledbadge_bitmap` and the `image_upload` feature above describe. This entity was bound `set_text: write_badge_data`, a role name no consumer's vocabulary contains, pointing at a parameterless chunk write; it resolved nothing and drew nothing, while reading as though a text control existed. Brightness stays in `features` because the header does carry it — the uploader sets it, not a slider on this entity.

remaining_unknowns: Whether the badge rejects or misbehaves on a zero date (bytes 38-43) is untested — every known client sends the current time, so the `default: 0` on those parameters is a filler value nobody has exercised.
The speed nibble (byte 8 bits 4-7) cannot be declared as its own parameter because it shares a byte with `mode`; the template pins it at 0 (slowest).
Timing (3 s ack timeout, 300 ms first-chunk delay, 25 ms inter-chunk) is app-derived; Nilhcem/FOSSASIA use 100 ms between chunks and also work.

write_badge_data.description: The badge's one write: a 64-byte header followed by the stripe-major bitmap, sent as a stream of 16-byte acknowledged chunks (framing.max_chunk_size), 300 ms before the first data chunk and 25 ms between chunks. The template IS the 64-byte header with slot 1 parameterised and slots 2-8 empty, then the bitmap bytes; a multi-slot upload fills bytes 9-15 and 18-31 the same way for its other slots. Header layout: bytes 0-3 magic "wang"; 4 reserved 0; 5 brightness; 6 flash bits (bit N = slot N blinks); 7 marquee bits (bit N = slot N gets the animated border); 8-15 one speed+mode byte per slot, upper nibble speed 0-7 (slowest-fastest; the app shows it as 1-8), lower nibble mode; 16-31 per-slot message length, uint16 BIG-endian, in 8-pixel-wide stripes (= characters for text; Elektor's sniff of the vendor app sends 00 07 for "Welcome"); 32-37 zero; 38-43 date year&0xFF, month, day, hour, minute, second; 44-62 zero; 63 zero. Bitmap: the message split into 8-column stripes of `height` bytes (11/12/16), one byte per row, MSB = leftmost pixel, 1 = LED on. Sources: the Elektor Jan/Feb 2023 article (decompile + sniff of the same vendor app), fossasia/badgemagic-firmware BadgeBLE.md, Nilhcem's and Doridian's converters, fossasia/led-name-badge-ls32. The one thing the vocabulary cannot say: speed and mode share byte 8, so `mode` here is the low nibble with the speed nibble at 0 (slowest); a handler composing (speed << 4) | mode takes the mode table from this parameter and the speed range from this note.

bitmap.description: Stripe-major bitmap: `length` stripes of `height` bytes each, MSB = leftmost pixel, 1 = on; zero-padded by the sender to a 16-byte chunk boundary. 8128 = the 8192-byte flash minus the header.

brightness.description: Byte 5. The vendor app always writes 0x00; the ls32 client exercises the other three (0x10/0x20/0x40).

flash.description: Byte 6: bit N set = slot N blinks.

length.description: Bytes 16-17: slot 1's message length in 8-pixel stripes = len(bitmap) / height. BIG-endian (Elektor sniff 00 07; Nilhcem, FOSSASIA, Doridian and BadgeBLE.md agree).

marquee.description: Byte 7: bit N set = slot N shows the animated border.

mode.description: Byte 8, slot 1's animation (low nibble); the speed nibble is 0 in this template. Table from BadgeBLE.md and ls32's --mode help; Elektor's sniff: speed 8 + scroll right = 0x71.

year.description: Byte 38: year & 0xFF. Every known client sends the current time; whether the badge cares is unverified (see remaining_unknowns).

characteristics.name: Badge Data
characteristics.notes: GATT properties are read+write+notify (Elektor Table 1, FOSSASIA BadgeBLE.md), but reads/notifications return nothing useful — the protocol is write-only in practice. checksum OMITTED: the device uses NO CRC/checksum (confirmed absent). length_prefix false: raw 16-byte chunks with no BLE-level length prefix.

services.name: Badge Secondary Service
services.notes: Second service present on the badge (Elektor Jan/Feb 2023, Table 1). Undocumented; the vendor app never references it.
